clue.text: Where you might shop for Dexter's new diverting books

indicators.note: made new, so the letters of the two words are put in a fresh order
turning aside from their course, so the books' letters are mixed in with the rest

parts.note: OT is the Old Testament, a collection of books of the Bible

explanation.surface: Someone might go shopping for Dexter's latest entertaining novels.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diverting' reads as amusing books, but with 'new' it scrambles OT along with FORDEXTERS; the two letters do not sit together in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Oxford Street is London's busiest retail street, lined with department stores and chain shops.

clue.text: Taking a Number 13, how busy, on average?

indicators.note: A bus taking a passenger holds them inside for the journey, so the letters here close round the piece named next instead of standing beside it.
A busy street has everything in it moving at once, and letters told they are busy will not stay where they were put.

parts.note: the figure is to be written out in full, all eight letters of it
three more letters, taken from the clue exactly as it prints them
A plus No., the everyday abbreviation for number, kept whole in the middle

explanation.surface: A passenger wonders how crowded the number 13 bus usually is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Number' does two jobs at once: it hands over its own abbreviation and it tells you the 13 beside it is to be written out as a word. The capital N is a bus route dressed up as a proper name.
explanation.definitionFit: on average → ONE WITH ANOTHER: an old idiom meaning taking one case together with the next, so it does the work of 'on average' in a sentence.

clue.text: When the tide goes out one might view such accommodation!

definitions.text: When the tide goes out one might view such
definitions.meaning: the wet sand and mud an estuary uncovers as the sea draws back goes by this same word

definitions.note: Accommodation is a mass noun in British use — nobody says accommodations — so it covers a row of homes as readily as one.
definitions.meaning: the ordinary British word for a home occupying one floor of a larger building

explanation.surface: At low tide you can see what sort of housing the shoreline has to offer.
explanation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark is the setter admitting there is no machinery here, only two senses of one word. Britain's tidal estuaries — the Wash, Morecambe Bay — are miles of the stuff the first half means.
explanation.definitionFit: accommodation → FLATS: a flat is a self-contained home on one floor, where Americans say apartment; the other sense is the mud an estuary uncovers.

clue.text: Striking Brazilian moorlands discovered on tour

indicators.note: Split it as dis-covered and it means stripped of its covers, so the letters at each end — the ones covering the rest — come off.
A side on tour is away from home and moving from place to place, which is what the letters do here.

parts.note: nine letters with the outermost one at each end taken off, leaving seven to work with

explanation.surface: A touring party comes upon some strikingly beautiful moorland in Brazil.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discovered' is the one worth learning: read as dis-covered it takes the outside letters off rather than finding anything. Brazil's footballers go by a single name, and 'striking' says which position this one played.
explanation.definitionFit: Striking Brazilian → RONALDO: Brazil's great No 9 of the 1990s, a striker by trade and, like most Brazilian footballers, known by one name alone.

clue.text: See 1
Pause when performing play of disreputable author

indicators.note: A piece of something is part of it and not the whole, which is the cue to read inside the words that follow rather than translate them.

parts.note: the letters run unbroken across the gap between the two words, starting some way into the first

explanation.surface: An actor breaks off mid-scene in a play by a writer of bad reputation.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing here shouts concealment: 'of' is the only signal, doing the work of 'part of'. In the theatre the word means the whole cast frozen in position, which is the pause the definition promises.
explanation.definitionFit: Pause when performing play → TABLEAU: the moment when the actors hold still in a posed group and the action stops dead, a staple of Victorian theatre and of pantomime.

clue.text: At times rocky, otherwise mountainous country

indicators.note: A rocky road is an uneven one that throws you about, and letters given a rocky ride do not land in the order they set off in.

parts.note: seven letters of raw material, the phrase taken exactly as it stands
'or otherwise' — the two words do the same job in a sentence, so one stands in for the other

explanation.surface: The going is rocky in places and mountainous everywhere else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'At times' reads as an adverb setting up 'rocky' and is seven of the nine letters. The country is the eastern half of the island of Timor, independent of Indonesia since 2002 and almost all of it upland.
explanation.definitionFit: mountainous country → EAST TIMOR: a small south-east Asian nation built on a steep, rugged spine of mountains running the length of its half of the island.

clue.text: Film figure's piano recording's retained: 16 loses nothing

indicators.note: the recording is held within the word for figure

parts.note: to figure is to think or reckon
an EP is an extended-play record
p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly

indicators.note: the word for nothing is dropped from the cross-referenced answer

parts.note: the answer to 16, ANOTHER
O is the round symbol for nothing, zero

explanation.surface: A cinema figure's piano recording is kept, while some other number loses nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Film figure' looks like a single unit, but 'Film' alone is the definition and 'figure' means think. Removing O from ANOTHER leaves the big cat's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The Pink Panther is the 1963 Blake Edwards comedy starring Peter Sellers as Inspector Clouseau, and its sequels.

clue.text: Still preferring bishop to rook, extremely optimistically

indicators.note: On a chessboard a bishop is B and a rook R, and preferring the one to the other puts the B exactly where the R was standing.

parts.note: a thing that is still is at rest — six letters, one of which is about to be traded

explanation.surface: A chess player still rates the bishop above the rook, which is optimistic of them.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole trick is that 'Still' is not the adverb the sentence wants but a word meaning motionless, and chess supplies the two initials that change places.
explanation.definitionFit: extremely optimistically → AT BEST: the phrase marks the most favourable reading a thing will bear — 'at best a draw' — which is optimism at its limit.

clue.text: Personage perhaps lying in state is unknown for now

definitions.meaning: a dignitary's body on public view before the funeral: what is left of them, put there for people to file past
the everyday sense: nobody can say yet, and the matter waits on events

explanation.surface: A great man's body lies in state while some question about him stays unanswered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' is the signal that the first half is an instance and not a definition — one thing a body lying in state might be said to be doing. The hinge is 'lying', which the dead do and an open question does too.
explanation.definitionFit: is unknown for now → REMAINS TO BE SEEN: the idiom for a matter events have not yet settled; the other sense is a body put on public view.

clue.text: Day chosen for replacement of corps in retiring company, generating some power

parts.note: dies is Latin for day

indicators.note: the word for chosen goes in where the corps letter was
going back, so the word for company is turned backwards

parts.note: a circle is a group of people, a company
C is an abbreviation for corps in military use
elect means chosen, as in president-elect

explanation.surface: A chosen date for reorganising an army corps within a company that is in decline produces some energy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retiring' turns CIRCLE into ELCRIC; ELECT then takes the place of its first C to make the second half.
explanation.definitionFit: A diesel-electric system uses a diesel engine to drive a generator whose electricity powers the motors, as in locomotives.

clue.text: See 10
Keeping in touch, poorly Enigmatist's going to take a break

indicators.note: the rearranged letters hold the setter's contraction inside them
the letters of touch are in poor shape, so they are rearranged

parts.note: the setter speaking as I: I'll means I will, I am going to

explanation.surface: The setter, feeling ill while staying in touch, announces a rest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poorly' turns TOUCH into CHOUT, which holds ILL, the setter's I'LL without the apostrophe.
explanation.definitionFit: To chill out is slang for relaxing or calming down, so taking time off.

clue.text: Ultimately harmful combo, big effects if activated

definitions.text: Ultimately harmful combo, big effects if activated

indicators.note: Something activated goes off, and what goes off does not leave its parts lying where they were.
Ultimately means in the end, and the end of a written word is the single letter it finishes on.

parts.note: the final letter of the word, the one 'ultimately' points at
eight more letters, taken from the clue as they stand

explanation.surface: A mixture that does harm in the end, with big consequences once it is set off.
explanation.walkthrough: Every word here counts twice, describing the thing and handing over its letters in the same breath. What it describes is code planted quietly in a system to go off on a date or an event.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight the clue describes the thing itself: malicious code that sits harmless in a system until some condition fires it, and then does real damage.

clue.text: Ruin preparation of minute steak: two internationals sacked

indicators.note: Preparing a dish means cutting it up and putting it together another way, which is what becomes of these letters.
Sacked players are dropped from the side, so the letters that stand for them leave the raw material.

parts.note: eleven letters of raw material before anything is dropped
I is the abbreviation for international, and at cricket an international match is a Test: both sets of letters come out

explanation.surface: A minute steak is being prepared on the day two international players are dropped.
explanation.walkthrough: Two senses of 'international' are wanted at once, the abbreviation and cricket's word for a match between countries, and both are lurking in the steak. Six letters are left, and 'preparation' shuffles them.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruin → UNMAKE: to unmake a thing is to undo the making of it, and what has been unmade is ruined as surely as if it had been smashed.

clue.text: Cover one's tracks maybe to achieve objective

indicators.note: Maybe flags an example rather than a definition: this is one of the things a track gets covered with, not the word for all of them.

parts.note: the black stuff spread over a road surface, which is one way a track gets covered
to get a result is to achieve it

explanation.surface: Someone hides the traces of where they have been in order to get what they want.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cover one's tracks' is a whole idiom in the surface, meaning to hide your traces, and the clue wants it literally instead — the stuff a track is covered with. 'To' joins the halves and adds nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: objective → TARGET: the thing being aimed at, whether a mark on a range or the figure a department has to hit by the end of the year.

clue.text: See 1
Fire obsessive bouncer for pinching clubber's bottom

indicators.note: Pinching here is gripping between finger and thumb rather than stealing, so the word closes on the letter and keeps it inside.

parts.note: the tiger in Winnie-the-Pooh who cannot stop bouncing, since bouncing is what Tiggers do best

indicators.note: The bottom of a word is the letter it ends on, which in a down entry is also the one sitting lowest in the grid.

parts.note: the last letter of that word

explanation.surface: A doorman with a fixation is being sacked for pinching a clubber's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a nightclub sacking, and 'Fire' looks like the verb doing the sacking. It is the definition instead, and the rest of the sentence turns out to be a children's book.
explanation.definitionFit: Fire → TRIGGER: to trigger something is to set it off, which is what firing a gun does, and both words take an object the same way.

clue.text: Very good supports covering us when blasting?

definitions.text: Very good supports covering us when blasting?

parts.note: pi, short for pious, is the crossword sense of very good

indicators.note: the shuffled supports must also cover the letters of us, which are then removed
blown apart, so the remaining letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Sturdy props hold up the roof over our heads while explosives go off.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove US from SUPPORTS and rearrange the rest; the whole clue also describes the answer, timbers in a mine where blasting is done.
explanation.definitionFit: Pit props are timber posts holding up the roof of a coal mine, protecting miners underneath during blasting.

clue.text: School's out when psychologist waves pen

indicators.note: When school is out everyone in it has left, and the six letters spelling it leave the longer word.
A wave runs through a thing and leaves it rippling, so the letters it passes through settle in a different order.

parts.note: twelve letters, and the word the whole clue works on
all six of these letters are present in the longer word, and they are the ones that go

explanation.surface: A psychologist waves a pen about now that school has finished for the day.
explanation.walkthrough: A school of thought is the tempting reading, and it is really a plain deletion: the six letters of 'school' come out of the psychologist. The pen left at the end is an animal's, not a writer's.
explanation.definitionFit: pen → PIGSTY: a pen is any small enclosure for livestock, and this is the one pigs are kept in, walled and roofed at one end.

clue.text: This bar's swinging ex-Palace favourite who likes scoring after gin

definitions.note: The definition is a whole statement rather than a noun: the answer is the swinging bar the clue is pointing at, and 'this' does the pointing.

indicators.note: In a down entry what comes after a thing sits below it, so the footballer goes underneath the snare rather than in front of it.

parts.note: a gin is a snare for catching game, nothing to do with the drink a bar would pour
Eberechi Eze, the goalscoring midfielder who left Crystal Palace, the south London club everyone calls Palace

explanation.surface: The bar is lively tonight, with a former Palace star who likes to score among the crowd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scoring' keeps the surface in the nightclub while pointing at goals, and the footballer's short name is the piece nobody sees coming. A gin here is the old trapper's snare.
explanation.definitionFit: This bar’s swinging → TRAPEZE: the horizontal bar hung from two ropes that a circus acrobat swings on, so the clue's sentence is literally true of it.

clue.text: See 7
A cracking feature set into low floor in the middle of a lounge?

definitions.note: The clue offers a noun, a spell of lounging, where the answer is the -ing form of a verb; both name the same idle activity.

indicators.note: A crack splits a thing open along its length, so the letter named goes into the split rather than onto either end.
This says where: between the two pieces already named, not in front of them or behind.
What is set into something is fixed inside it, the way a stone is set into a ring.

parts.note: the noise cattle make: cows low in the byre
a feature of a face, the one that juts out at the bottom of it
the ground is the floor you stand on out of doors, and it is the word that gets cracked open
the clue's own opening word, taken as the single letter it is

explanation.surface: An estate agent points out a cracking feature set into the low floor of a lounge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cracking' is the estate agent's word for excellent in the surface and a physical split in the wordplay. 'Low' is the cow's noise, one of the crossword's standing tricks, and the floor meant is out of doors.
explanation.definitionFit: a lounge → MOOCHING AROUND: to mooch around is to drift about with nothing much to do, which is what a lounge about amounts to.

clue.text: See 21
There but for all to see, our most prominent, looking skyward?

definitions.text: There but for all to see, our most prominent, looking skyward?

indicators.note: means except, so our is taken without that letter

parts.note: U is the British film certificate for universal viewing

indicators.note: in a down clue, the letters read upwards, towards the sky

parts.note: No. 1, written as NO with I for one, the most prominent

explanation.surface: Something up there, visible to everyone, is our most conspicuous sight in the night sky.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue describes the answer too: the constellation is there for all to see, looking up. NO I read upwards gives ION.
explanation.definitionFit: Orion, the Hunter, is among the most conspicuous constellations in the night sky, seen across the world.

clue.text: Considered Scotswoman correct to hide face away from sundown to sunrise

indicators.note: the word for considered hides that front letter inside it

parts.note: thought means considered, as a past tense
the front letter of the word for correct
hen is a Scottish informal term of address for a woman

indicators.note: the face of the word for correct is moved away, leaving the rest

parts.note: right means correct

explanation.surface: A thoughtful Scottish woman is right to hide her face after dark.
explanation.walkthrough: RIGHT loses its face R, which goes into THOUGHT as THROUGHT; HEN and IGHT follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Through the night means for the whole of the hours of darkness, dusk till dawn.

clue.text: Top director, top tester and theatre's top checker

indicators.note: the top letter of the word for tester is cut off

parts.note: a prober is someone who probes, testing or investigating

indicators.note: only the top, first, letter of the word is taken

parts.note: the word is used for its first letter
a reiner is one who reins in, checking or restraining

explanation.surface: A list of leading figures: a director, a tester and a theatre's chief inspector.
explanation.walkthrough: The three 'top's do three jobs: part of the definition, cutting the head off PROBER, and picking T from 'theatre's'.
explanation.definitionFit: Rob Reiner is an American film director of When Harry Met Sally and This Is Spinal Tap.

clue.text: See 25
